description: Team Concorde brings together curious minds passionate about space exploration, aerospace engineering, and technology. With interests in engineering, software, and design, we aim to turn NASA’s open data into innovative solutions. We’re looking for teammates skilled in programming, AI/ML, data science, design, and research who love collaboration, creativity, and solving real-world challenges.
summary:
Concordemoon is a web app that helps users compare landing sites and dates on the Moon. At the lunar south pole, the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon and the Earth appears low in the sky. This means that even a small ridge can block a lander's solar power or its direct radio link. Tools to calculate these conditions already exist, but they are usually designed for experts and spread across different platforms.

Concordemoon brings these tools together in one place. A 3D Moon globe with NASA maps lets users select an existing site or any point on the lunar surface. The Horizon view shows what the terrain looks like from the surface and, hour by hour, whether it blocks the Sun (power) or the Earth (communication). A dashboard and comparison page help users evaluate up to three sites and dates based on different goals: power, communications, safe landing or a balance between them. Users can also set their own requirements for sunlight, Earth link and slope.

All calculations use NASA data (JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA terrain) and are checked against published results. It is a planning tool, not flight software.
details:
What it does

Concordemoon has four main pages.

  • Orbital view. A 3D Moon globe with NASA Moon Trek maps: photo mosaic, hillshade, elevation, slope and temperature. Users can select one of nine registered sites (Shackleton rim, Connecting Ridge C1 and C2, Mons Mouton, Malapert A, Schrödinger Basin, Apollo 11, 16 and 17) or click anywhere on the Moon and save that location as a pin. Requirement sliders (Sun during the stay, Earth link, slope) show which areas of the Moon and south pole zones meet the selected conditions in green or gray.
  • Horizon view. A first-person 3D view from the lunar surface, built using NASA LOLA elevation data, with the real positions of the Sun, Earth and star sky. Users select a date and a stay length. The panel shows when the Sun and Earth rise and set behind the actual terrain, as well as the percentage of the stay with power and a direct communication link.
  • Dashboard. For the selected site or saved pin, it shows: Sun and Earth gauges, countdowns to the next sunrise and earthrise, an hour-by-hour chart of the stay, a 90-day sunlight heatmap, and a check against the user's requirements. It also ranks all sites and pins based on a selected goal and allows users to export the ranking as a CSV.
  • Compare sites. Users can select up to three saved points or sites. Each one gets a score card with a horizon preview and a radar chart showing power, communication, continuity and slope. Users can also compare the same point across different dates.

An optional AI assistant answers questions in English or Spanish and can help users navigate the app. It uses the app's own data tools, and its numbers are checked before being shown.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth positions: NASA/JPL Horizons, with hourly data for 90 days (2026-11-14 to 2027-02-12 UTC).
    • South of 86°S: the LOLA 20 m south pole model (NASA Goddard PGDA, 200 km area).
    • Anywhere up to 80° N/S: the LOLA global 118 m model (50 km area).
    • The horizon is calculated every 0.25° of azimuth from 2 m above the ground, representing the height of a lander's solar panel.
  • Visibility: the app compares the Sun and Earth discs with the terrain horizon. This allows us to calculate the percentage of each hour with sunlight and a direct communication link.
  • Validation: results are compared with Gläser et al. 2018 (sunlight at Shackleton and the connecting ridge) and the Horizons web app.
  • Points anywhere on the Moon: these are calculated in the browser using terrain tiles generated from NASA data and served through Cloudflare.

Benefits and intended impact

  • One platform brings together information that normally requires several expert tools and helps answer the question: "Will this site have power and a link to Earth on these dates?"
  • Mission planners, students and the general public can compare sites and dates in just a few minutes. They can also see why a location meets or fails certain conditions, such as terrain blocking the Sun or Earth, instead of only seeing a number.
  • Users can set their own requirements, allowing the same data to be used for different goals, including power, communications or a suitable landing slope.

Tools and languages

  • TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS.
  • CesiumJS (3D globe) and three.js with React Three Fiber (Horizon view).
  • Python scripts to download and prepare the NASA data.
  • Web Workers to calculate terrain in the browser.
  • Cloudflare R2 and Workers for terrain tiles; Vercel for hosting.
  • Optional AI assistant: Google Gemini and Groq models, through a server function.

What makes it creative

  • The visual information and calculations come from the same NASA data. For example, when the Earth disappears behind a ridge in the 3D view, the communication indicator drops at that same hour.
  • It allows users to explore any point on the Moon, instead of only working with a list of prepared sites.
  • Features like goal-based scoring, one-click comparison of the same location on a different date, and the sunlight heatmap make it easier to understand the differences between potential landing sites.
  • The AI assistant makes the platform more interactive. Users can ask questions in natural language, request information about landing sites, and interact with the app through the assistant, which can navigate and control different features based on their requests. The assistant also supports voice input, allowing users to speak their questions and give voice commands instead of having to type everything.

Factors the team considered

  • Validity first: we wanted every value to come from a public and traceable source and be checked against other results. We also list known limitations, such as the 118 m model not showing smaller ridges.
  • Planning aid, not flight grade: rocks, small craters and dust are not included in the data, so green means "meets your requirements", not "safe".
    • Color is never the only way to show information; symbols and text are also included.
    • The app supports English and Spanish through the assistant.

LRO LOLA 20 m south pole DEM (LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ), NASA Goddard PGDA, Barker et al. 2023
LRO LOLA global DEM 118 m (USGS Astrogeology)
NASA Moon Trek (LRO WAC mosaic, LOLA hillshade and slope, Diviner temperature)
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio: Deep Star Maps (star sky)
NASA SVS: Tour of the Moon 4K (landing page video)
NASA Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS missions per site)
